title: Packer and Ansible: building the sandbox image

story: Nova's run claims a fresh VM. If that VM starts as plain Ubuntu, the run first installs Docker, Node 24, Python and uv, clones fcp, fills the npm cache, downloads Chromium for Playwright and builds FCP Lab with its fake data. That is many minutes of the same work in every run, paid at full VM price, and two VMs that start an hour apart can even get different package versions.

So we do that work once, ahead of time, and save the result. But that creates a new risk. If last night's saved machine has a broken Node install, every run tomorrow morning breaks at the same moment, on every ticket.
hook.question: How do we do the slow setup once, and make sure a broken setup never reaches the runs?

p: An AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is a saved copy of a machine's disk. Every EC2 VM starts from one, the way every container starts from a Docker image. Baking means preparing a machine with everything a run needs and saving its disk as a new AMI. After that, a run's VM starts with the tools, caches and FCP Lab already there.

Packer is the tool that bakes. It reads a template in HCL, the same language as OpenTofu. A source block says how to get a temporary machine: amazon-ebs starts an EC2 VM from a base image, here our own Ubuntu 24 image. A build block lists provisioners, the steps that change that machine, and ours runs an Ansible playbook. When the steps finish, Packer saves the disk as a new AMI and deletes the temporary VM.

If you know Docker, this is a Dockerfile and docker build for a whole VM. The comparison stops at speed: an AMI has no layers and no cache, so every build starts from the base image again and takes many minutes. That is one reason we build at night, when nobody waits for it.

code.file: sandbox.pkr.hcl (a simplified, single-file version of our template)

notes.text: The channel goes into the image name. A testing image that is never promoted expires after 72 hours.
amazon-ebs: start an EC2 VM, run the steps, save its disk as an AMI.
The build machine is big for speed. The same AMI later runs lite, full and wide VMs; the size is only the instance type.
Start from the newest release of our own Ubuntu 24 base image.
The provisioner: Ansible changes the temporary VM before Packer saves it.

read.h: Ansible: describe the machine, not the steps
p: Ansible is the tool that changes the machine. Its file is a playbook, which runs roles on hosts, and a role is a folder of tasks. A task does not say "run useradd". It calls a module with the state you want: the user agent exists with uid 1001. The module checks the machine first. If the state is already true, it reports ok and changes nothing. If not, it makes the change and reports changed.

That property is called idempotence: running the same playbook twice gives the same machine, and the second run reports changed=0. It matters more than it sounds. A nightly build that fails halfway can simply run again, and the same role can run on a machine that already has half of it. The test is easy, and you will do it in the lab: run the playbook twice and read the last line. If the second run says changed=1, one task is not describing a state. It is repeating an action, such as appending a line to a file every time.

code.text:
- name: Create the non-root user the harness runs as
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: agent
    uid: 1001
    shell: /bin/bash

- name: Send all web traffic through the egress proxy
  ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
    path: /etc/environment
    line: "{{ item }}"
  loop:
    - HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.ai-agents.example.com:3128
    - NO_PROXY=.amazonaws.com,.ai-agents.example.com

notes.text: A module and the state you want. If the user already exists like this, nothing happens.
lineinfile: make sure this exact line is in the file. A second run finds it and changes nothing.
loop runs the task once per item; {{ item }} is the current one.

read.see:
$ ansible-playbook ... playbook.yml        # second run
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
image-lab                  : ok=3    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0

p: A freshly baked image is not used yet. Every night the workflow builds it on the testing channel. Then comes a smoke test, a short check of the few things that must work: it boots one VM from the new image and checks that the harness starts (nova-worker --version) and that FCP Lab passes one real Playwright spec. The smoke VM is always destroyed, pass or fail.

The launch templates never name an AMI directly. They read it from a parameter in AWS Systems Manager (SSM), /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id, every time a VM starts. So promoting an image is two writes: copy the current value to ami-id-previous, then write the new AMI's ID into ami-id. No HCL changes and no apply. If the smoke test fails, nothing is promoted, runs keep the image they had, and the testing image expires by itself.

Rollback is the same move backwards: write ami-id-previous into ami-id, one command that a person runs. VMs that are already warm still run the bad image until they are replaced. The sweeper replaces warm VMs older than 24 hours, and a person can terminate them at once if it is urgent.

code.file: the promote step of the nightly workflow, and the rollback
code.text:
# Smoke test passed: keep the current image as "previous", then point at the new one.
prev=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id --query Parameter.Value --output text)
aws ssm put-parameter --name /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id-previous --value "$prev" --overwrite
aws ssm put-parameter --name /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id --value "$AMI" --overwrite

# Rollback, run by a person: point back at the previous image.
prev=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id-previous --query Parameter.Value --output text)
aws ssm put-parameter --name /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id --value "$prev" --overwrite

notes.text: Read the image that runs today.
$AMI is tonight's image, which just passed the smoke test. New VMs use it from now on.
Rollback writes the previous image back. Nothing is rebuilt.

deeper.h: Go deeper: what our image holds
p: The first part of the role installs the toolchain: Docker with compose, Node 24, Python 3.13 and uv, git and jq. It creates the agent user, blocks the instance metadata service for everyone except root, installs a small timer that watches for Spot interruption notices, and turns off automatic upgrades, because the image is rebuilt every night instead.

The heavy part bakes a git mirror of fcp, the npm and uv caches, Playwright's Chromium, FCP Lab with its images built and fake seed data in place, a pinned Claude Code, our plugins and the nova-worker harness. It ends by writing /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json with the lockfile hashes and versions, so a run can reinstall only what changed since the image was baked.

lab.title: Bake, smoke-test, promote and roll back an image
needs: Docker running. A container stands in for the EC2 build VM, docker commit for "save the disk as an AMI", and an image tag for the SSM parameter.
Ansible with the community.docker collection (ansible-galaxy collection list | grep community.docker).
Optional, for the last step: the hashicorp/packer:1.14 Docker image (about 100 MB), or Packer itself.
lab.goal: Run an Ansible role on a stand-in build machine twice, save it as an image, smoke-test it, promote it with a pointer, and roll back with the same pointer.

guess.q: You run the playbook on a fresh machine and the recap says changed=2. You run the exact same playbook on the same machine again. What should the recap say?

options.text: changed=2 again, because the same tasks ran again.
options.why: The tasks ran, but each module checked the machine first and found the state already true, so nothing changed.

options.text: changed=0, because every task finds its state already in place.
options.why: That is idempotence. A second run that changes something means a task repeats an action instead of describing a state.

options.text: failed=1, because the user agent already exists.
options.why: ansible.builtin.user describes a state: the user exists. Finding it already there is success, not an error.

follow.say: Make the lab folder and paste this block, because it writes a playbook and a small copy of our image role with two tasks. Then let Ansible check the syntax.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p4-4 && cd ~/academy-labs/p4-4
mkdir -p roles/ai_agent_sandbox/tasks
cat > playbook.yml <<'EOF'
- name: Lab copy of the ai-agent-sandbox image
  hosts: all
  roles:
    - ai_agent_sandbox
EOF
cat > roles/ai_agent_sandbox/tasks/main.yml <<'EOF'
- name: Create the non-root user the harness runs as
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: agent
    uid: 1001
    shell: /bin/bash

- name: Send all web traffic through the egress proxy
  ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
    path: /etc/environment
    line: "{{ item }}"
  loop:
    - HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.ai-agents.example.com:3128
    - NO_PROXY=.amazonaws.com,.ai-agents.example.com
EOF
ansible-playbook --syntax-check -i localhost, playbook.yml

follow.say: Start the build machine. Packer would start an EC2 VM from our base image; here a container from python:3.13-slim plays that part (Ansible needs Python on the machine).
follow.do: docker run -d --name image-lab python:3.13-slim sleep infinity

follow.say: Run the role on it. -c community.docker.docker tells Ansible to reach the host through docker exec instead of SSH.
follow.see:
TASK [ai_agent_sandbox : Create the non-root user the harness runs as] *********
changed: [image-lab]

TASK [ai_agent_sandbox : Send all web traffic through the egress proxy] ********
changed: [image-lab] => (item=HTTPS_PROXY=http://proxy.ai-agents.example.com:3128)
changed: [image-lab] => (item=NO_PROXY=.amazonaws.com,.ai-agents.example.com)

image-lab                  : ok=3    changed=2    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0

follow.say: Run exactly the same command again, because the second run is the idempotence test.
follow.see: image-lab                  : ok=3    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0

follow.say: Bake: save the machine as an image on the testing channel, then delete the build machine, which is what Packer does as its last two steps.
follow.do: docker commit image-lab ai-agent-sandbox:testing-1 && docker rm -f image-lab

follow.say: Smoke-test the new image on a fresh machine started from it, because only proof earns a promotion.
follow.do: docker run --rm ai-agent-sandbox:testing-1 sh -c 'id agent && grep -c PROXY /etc/environment'

follow.say: Promote: point release at the tested image. From now on, anything that starts from ai-agent-sandbox:release gets it, the way launch templates read the SSM parameter.
follow.do:
docker tag ai-agent-sandbox:testing-1 ai-agent-sandbox:release
docker images ai-agent-sandbox --format 'table {{.Tag}}\t{{.ID}}'
follow.see:
TAG         IMAGE ID
release     b74fdad97b1e
testing-1   b74fdad97b1e

follow.say: Optional: save the Packer template from the Understand step as sandbox.pkr.hcl and let Packer check it, so you have read and validated the real recipe's shape. -syntax-only needs no plugins and no AWS account.
follow.see: Syntax-only check passed. Everything looks okay.

lab.build:
Bake build 2 with a manifest, promote it, then roll it back. Add the two manifest tasks below to the end of roles/ai_agent_sandbox/tasks/main.yml: a folder /etc/ai-agent-sandbox and a file manifest.json in it that records the build number. Start a new build machine from python:3.13-slim (each night starts from the base image, never from yesterday's image), run the playbook twice with -e build=2, and bake it as ai-agent-sandbox:testing-2. Smoke-test it by reading the manifest. Promote it the way the workflow does: first tag the current release as previous, then tag testing-2 as release. Finally, pretend build 2 is bad and roll back by tagging previous as release.

- name: Make the manifest folder
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: /etc/ai-agent-sandbox
    state: directory
    mode: "0755"

- name: Record what is in the image
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    dest: /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json
    content: "{{ {'image': 'ai-agent-sandbox', 'build': build} | to_nice_json }}"
    mode: "0644"
checks: The second playbook run on the new build machine says changed=0, with ok=5.
Right after promoting, docker images shows release and testing-2 with the same IMAGE ID, and previous with testing-1's ID.

After the rollback, release has testing-1's ID again, and docker run --rm ai-agent-sandbox:release cat /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json fails with No such file or directory, because build 1 had no manifest.
Nothing was rebuilt during the rollback: only a tag moved.

solution.text:
# roles/ai_agent_sandbox/tasks/main.yml: add at the end
- name: Make the manifest folder
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: /etc/ai-agent-sandbox
    state: directory
    mode: "0755"

- name: Record what is in the image
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    dest: /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json
    content: "{{ {'image': 'ai-agent-sandbox', 'build': build} | to_nice_json }}"
    mode: "0644"

# then, in the lab folder:
docker run -d --name image-lab python:3.13-slim sleep infinity
ansible-playbook -i 'image-lab,' -c community.docker.docker -e ansible_python_interpreter=auto_silent playbook.yml -e build=2
ansible-playbook -i 'image-lab,' -c community.docker.docker -e ansible_python_interpreter=auto_silent playbook.yml -e build=2          # changed=0
docker commit image-lab ai-agent-sandbox:testing-2 && docker rm -f image-lab
docker run --rm ai-agent-sandbox:testing-2 cat /etc/ai-agent-sandbox/manifest.json   # smoke test
docker tag ai-agent-sandbox:release ai-agent-sandbox:previous                        # promote
docker tag ai-agent-sandbox:testing-2 ai-agent-sandbox:release
docker tag ai-agent-sandbox:previous ai-agent-sandbox:release                        # roll back

lab.fix: A teammate finds lineinfile too long and replaces the proxy task with ansible.builtin.shell running two echo "..." >> /etc/environment lines. Make that change, start a fresh build machine and run the playbook twice: the second recap says changed=1, and docker exec image-lab cat /etc/environment shows every proxy line twice. On a machine baked after a retried build, the environment would grow with every retry. Put lineinfile back, and prove it with two runs on a fresh machine: changed=0 the second time.
explain: Why do we bake the slow setup into an image instead of running it at the start of each run?
What does changed=0 on a second Ansible run prove, and what does changed=1 tell you?
Why can promotion and rollback each be one small write, and what still runs the old image after a rollback?
lab.done: You promoted build 2, rolled back to build 1 by moving a tag, and removed the lab images with docker rmi ai-agent-sandbox:testing-1 ai-agent-sandbox:testing-2 ai-agent-sandbox:release ai-agent-sandbox:previous.

check.q: Tonight's image fails the smoke test: one Playwright spec in FCP Lab does not pass. What do Nova's runs use tomorrow morning?

options.text: Tonight's image, because it is the newest one.
options.why: New VMs start from whatever the parameter points at, and only a passing smoke test moves it.

options.text: Nothing: runs wait until a person fixes the image.
options.why: Nothing about the current image changed, so runs go on as normal.

options.text: The same image as today, because nothing was promoted; tonight's image stays on testing and expires by itself.
options.why: That is why the pointer exists: a broken build never reaches a run, and nobody has to clean it up.

check.q: You run the image playbook twice on the same machine, and the second recap says changed=1 on the task that writes the proxy settings. What does it tell you?

options.text: That task repeats an action, probably appending a line, instead of describing a state, so every run adds another copy.
options.why: An idempotent task finds its state already true on the second run. Use a module that describes the state, such as lineinfile.

options.text: Nothing important: Ansible always reports one change on the second run.
options.why: A healthy playbook reports changed=0 on the second run. Any change is a task to look at.

options.text: The machine drifted between the two runs.
options.why: Nothing else touched the machine between two back-to-back runs. The task itself made the change.

check.q: At 10:00 people report that every new sandbox fails to start FCP Lab, since last night's promotion. What is the fastest safe fix?

options.text: Change image_id in the launch templates in HCL, plan and apply.
options.why: That takes a PR, a plan and an apply. The launch templates read the image from the parameter exactly so that this is not needed.

options.text: Write ami-id-previous back into /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id, then replace the warm VMs that run the bad image.
options.why: Rollback is one write. New VMs get the previous image at once, and warm VMs are recycled by the sweeper within a day or terminated by hand.

options.text: Fix the role and wait for tonight's build.
options.why: Fix the role too, but runs would stay broken all day. Roll back first, then fix.

p: Our images are built from the infrastructure repo's packer/ folder: one shared template for every image, packer/images/ai-agent-sandbox/ with its packer_vars.hcl and playbook.yml, and the role packer/ansible/roles/ai_agent_sandbox/. The image starts from rhino-base-ubuntu-24, builds on an m8i.2xlarge with a 120 GiB disk in the inf account, and is shared with the ai-agents account. Image names follow rhino-<image>-v<N>-<testing|release>-<timestamp>.

A nightly workflow, build-ai-agent-sandbox.yml, builds on the testing channel, boots one VM from the full launch template, runs nova-worker --version and FCP Lab's not-found-page Playwright spec over SSM, always terminates the VM, and on a pass moves /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id (keeping ami-id-previous). A failure posts the lab report to #ai-agents-alerts, our Slack channel for platform alerts. A person owns the workflow; agents never dispatch workflows.

tickets.why: The image's base: toolchain, the agent user, the metadata lock, spot-watch, unattended upgrades off.
The heavy bake: fcp mirror, caches, Chromium, FCP Lab, Claude Code, plugins, nova-worker and the manifest.
The nightly build, the smoke test, promotion through the SSM parameter and one-command rollback.
The launch templates read image_id from resolve:ssm:/ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id, which makes promotion a pointer move.

words.plain: Amazon Machine Image: a saved copy of a machine's disk that new EC2 VMs start from.
A tool that starts a temporary machine, runs provisioners on it, and saves the result as an image.
A step in a Packer build that changes the temporary machine, for example running an Ansible playbook.
Safe to run again: the second run finds the state already in place and changes nothing (changed=0).
Point the SSM parameter that launch templates read at a tested image; the old value is kept for rollback.

review.q: List the four stages of the nightly image in order, and say what happens to the image when stage three fails.
review.a: Build (Packer and Ansible) on the testing channel, smoke test on one VM, promote by moving the SSM parameter, and roll back if needed. If the smoke test fails, nothing is promoted and the testing image expires after 72 hours.

review.q: Rewrite this task so it is idempotent: shell: echo "HTTPS_PROXY=..." >> /etc/environment
review.a: ansible.builtin.lineinfile with path: /etc/environment and line: "HTTPS_PROXY=...", which adds the line only if it is not there.

review.q: After a rollback, why can some VMs still run the bad image, and what replaces them?
review.a: Warm VMs were started from the bad image before the rollback. The sweeper recycles warm VMs older than 24 hours, or a person terminates them at once.

remember: Bake the slow setup once with an idempotent recipe, and let only a tested image move the pointer that every new VM reads.
